crop.name: Winter squash / pumpkin (Cucurbita, most consistent with a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima or C. pepo bush squash) — a single vining plant with two fruit set
crop.distinguishing_features: Very large palmate-lobed leaves with coarse, jagged-toothed margins, a dense pale reticulate vein network, and a bristly/hispid surface with fine white flecking; thick, hollow, deeply ribbed and prickly-hairy petioles and vine stems radiating from one crown; coiling branched tendrils at the nodes; two round fruit — one small pale-green immature fruit with darker mottled stripes still bearing a shriveled brown flower remnant at its tip, and one larger flattened-globe fruit with very dark green skin, pale green longitudinal stripes and white speckling, resting directly on the straw mulch

weeds.name: Grass seedlings / volunteer grass (crabgrass- or barnyardgrass-type annual grass, plus possible volunteer cereal from the straw)
weeds.distinguishing_features: Narrow strap-shaped blades with parallel venation and no branching veins, a keeled midrib, smooth hairless glossy surfaces, and blades emerging in tufts from thin round jointed culms at ground level; totally unlike the broad, netted-veined, hairy squash foliage. They are the most abundant weed, threading up through the squash canopy and across the fruit.

weeds.name: Purslane (Portulaca oleracea)
weeds.distinguishing_features: Low, prostrate, succulent rosettes with fleshy, smooth, spoon-shaped/obovate leaves clustered at the stem tips, thickened reddish-tinged stems, no hairs and no visible vein network — a fat, waxy look that contrasts sharply with the thin, hairy, sharply lobed squash leaves.

weeds.name: Broadleaf seedlings with scalloped/crenate round leaves (mallow- or ground-ivy/henbit-type, and a small clover-leaved seedling)
weeds.distinguishing_features: Small rounded to kidney-shaped leaves with blunt scalloped margins on slender petioles, growing in tiny low clusters on the bare mulched soil away from the squash crown; leaf size a fraction of even the youngest squash leaf, margins rounded rather than jaggedly toothed, and no tendrils or hollow ribbed stems.

non_plant_material: Dry straw/hay mulch covering most of the soil surface (bleached stems, chaff and broken stalks)
Bare dry soil and small clods visible between mulch straws
Dried, shriveled brown squash flower remnants attached to the young fruit and lying on the mulch
A small white/grey feather or downy fluff caught in the mulch
Dead, senesced brown leaf and stem debris
Deep cast shadows across leaves and mulch from strong direct sunlight
scene.hard_to_tell_apart: The hardest calls are (1) grass blades that lie directly across squash leaves and the fruit — at a glance the thin green strap merges into the leaf beneath it, and only the parallel venation and hard-edged straight margin separate them; (2) young, still-folded squash leaves near the crown, which are pale, crumpled and small enough to be mistaken for a broadleaf weed seedling until you trace their petiole back to the main vine; (3) the pale green squash tendrils versus fine grass leaf tips of the same width and colour; and (4) distinguishing genuine annual weed grass from volunteer cereal grass sprouting out of the straw mulch itself — visually they are nearly the same, though both are unwanted here.

"scene_notes": "A close, sunlit overhead view of one squash hill in a mulched home vegetable bed, shot mid-season. A single squash plant occupies most of the frame: its crown sits centre-right, with thick prickly petioles fanning outward and huge lobed leaves overhanging the edges of the photograph, so several tiles show nothing but squash leaf blade at full resolution. Two fruit are present — a small young one at the crown and a larger dark green striped one lying on the mulch below it. The gardener has mulched heavily with straw, which suppresses most weeds: the open ground is mostly bare straw with only scattered seedlings. Weed pressure is concentrated in two forms — grass, which is widespread and grows up through and over the crop, including blades draped across the fruit, and a patch of small broadleaf/succulent seedlings (purslane plus scalloped-leaved seedlings) on the open mulch away from the plant. Strong low sunlight creates high-contrast shadows and blown-out highlights on the upper leaf surfaces, which flattens texture in places and makes some leaf edges hard to trace. Any region containing thick ribbed hairy stems, tendrils, large netted lobed leaves, or fruit belongs to the crop; narrow parallel-veined blades and small low rosettes on the mulch do not."
